questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish distance travelled from displacement
questions.stem: A patient walks from the waiting room to the pharmacy and then straight back to the waiting room, and I need to describe the trip in both ways.

options.text: The distance is zero and the displacement is the length of the path walked.
options.misconception: swaps the two quantities in the description

options.text: The distance is the whole path length and the displacement is zero.
The distance and the displacement are equal because the route is the same.
options.misconception: assumes equal lengths for a closed path

options.text: The distance is zero because the patient ended where they started.
options.misconception: uses the final position to set the distance

questions.explanation: Distance adds up every step of the path, so the trip out and back totals twice the one-way length. Displacement is the straight line from start to finish, which is zero when the patient returns to the same place.
questions.hint: One counts the path, the other the gap.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish speed from velocity
questions.stem: A patient's speedometer shows a steady 5 kilometres per hour while the treadmill belt runs backwards at 2 kilometres per hour.

options.text: The patient's velocity is 5 kilometres per hour relative to the belt.
options.misconception: treats the belt as part of the ground

options.text: The patient's speed is 7 kilometres per hour because the two add together.
options.misconception: adds belt speed to patient speed

options.text: The patient's speed is 3 kilometres per hour because the two subtract.
options.misconception: subtracts in the wrong direction

options.text: The speed is 5 kilometres per hour while the velocity depends on direction.

questions.explanation: Speed is how fast the patient moves relative to the belt, so the reading of 5 is the speed. Velocity includes direction, and a belt running backwards makes the velocity relative to the floor smaller than that.
questions.hint: One has direction, the other does not.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change in velocity as acceleration
questions.stem: On the treadmill log the patient's velocity rises from 0.8 metres per second to 2.4 metres per second over a period of 2 seconds.

options.text: The acceleration is 0.8 metres per second squared across that interval.
The acceleration is 3.2 metres per second because the velocity trebled.
options.misconception: reads a velocity change as acceleration

options.text: The acceleration is 2.4 metres per second squared, which is the final speed.
options.misconception: treats the final velocity as the acceleration

options.text: The acceleration is 2 seconds, since that is the length of the change.
options.misconception: confuses the time interval with the acceleration

questions.explanation: Acceleration is the change in velocity over the time taken, so 1.6 divided by 2 gives 0.8 metres per second squared. The final speed and the interval are inputs to that division, not results.
questions.hint: Change in velocity over time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the fall time of an object released from rest
questions.stem: For a step-off test I release a weight from rest at a ledge 19.6 metres above the floor, and I need the time it takes to reach the floor taking g as 9.8.
questions.explanation: The distance fallen is half of g times the time squared, so 19.6 equals 4.9 times the square of the time, giving a time of 2.0 seconds. Ignoring air resistance is what makes the square root exact here.
questions.hint: Use half of g times t squared.

options.misconception: reads a steeper slope as less speed

options.text: The patient's speed is steady, because the trace is a straight line.
options.misconception: ignores that the straight line changes slope

options.text: The patient's speed is rising, because a steeper slope covers more ground per second.
The patient's speed is rising, because the graph curves upward more sharply.
options.misconception: describes curvature instead of the slope

questions.explanation: On a position-time graph the slope at any point is the speed, so a trace that becomes steeper shows the patient covering more ground in each second. A straight line that changes steepness is not a constant speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Apply the definition of average speed
questions.stem: A patient's exercise log shows 300 metres covered in the first four minutes and 150 metres in the next two minutes.

options.text: The average speed is 6.0 metres per second, since 450 metres takes 6 minutes.
options.misconception: treats minutes as seconds

options.text: The average speed is 1.25 metres per second, since 450 metres takes 360 seconds.
The average speed is 1.5 metres per second, from averaging 300 and 150 over 4 and 2.
options.misconception: averages the two speeds instead of the whole trip

options.text: The average speed is 75 metres per second, since the two distances are added.
options.misconception: adds distances and ignores the time

questions.explanation: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time, so 450 metres over 360 seconds gives 1.25 metres per second. Averaging the two segment speeds would weight them equally rather than by time.

options.misconception: multiplies the final speed by the time directly

options.text: The distance is 25 metres, from half of 2 times the square of 5.

questions.explanation: With constant acceleration from rest the distance is half of a times the time squared, so half of 2 times 25 gives 25 metres. Using the final speed directly without halving it would double the answer.

options.misconception: uses the earliest interval to describe the last

The patient covered 6 metres, since the speed rose by 3 metres per second.
options.misconception: confuses a speed change with a distance

questions.explanation: Distance is the area under a velocity-time graph, so the rising triangular section from 0 to 3 metres per second over six seconds covers 9 metres, and the flat section adds nothing.

options.text: The speed is 4.5 metres per second, from 0.09 divided by 0.02.
The speed is 0.0022 metres per second, from dividing the interval by the gap.

options.text: The speed is 11 centimetres per second, from adding the gap and the interval.
options.misconception: adds the two quantities together

questions.explanation: Speed is the distance between marks over the time between them, so 0.09 metres over 0.02 seconds gives 4.5 metres per second. Multiplying instead of dividing would be wrong by a factor of a thousand.
questions.hint: Divide the gap by the time interval.

options.misconception: takes only the slower speed into the sum

options.misconception: takes only the faster speed into the sum

options.text: They will meet sooner than if both walked in the same direction.

options.misconception: ignores the air resistance that usually separates them

options.text: The gravitational acceleration is the same for both, so they fall together without air.

options.text: The heavier ball carries more momentum, so the two fall at the same rate.
options.misconception: confuses momentum with rate of fall
